title: The sneaker ad requests
scenario:
Your studio makes an AI-assisted ad for a sneaker brand. You use Nano Banana 2.1 for images and Veo 3.1 for video. The client sends four requests. The exhibit shows them, with lines copied from the vendors' pages on 2026-10-06.

You are not a lawyer, and this case does not ask for legal advice. It asks what the vendor policies and docs say.
exhibit:
Client requests
  A. Put the face of a famous basketball player in the ad.
     We have no deal with him. Don't mention it's AI.
  B. Use 10 photos from a stock site as style references.
     We have not licensed them yet.
  C. Turn our own product photos (our studio shot them)
     into an 8-second video of the shoe turning.
  D. Remove the AI metadata from the final images
     so we can say our designers made them by hand.

Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy
  - "Violates the rights of others, including privacy and
    intellectual property rights"
  - "Impersonating an individual (living or dead) without
    explicit disclosure, in order to deceive"
  - "Misrepresenting the provenance of generated content by
    claiming it was created solely by a human, in order to deceive"
  - "Circumvention of abuse protections or safety filters"

Gemini API image docs
  "Make sure you have the necessary rights to any images you upload."
  "All generated images include a SynthID watermark."

Veo 3.1 docs
  "Prompts that violate our terms and guidelines are blocked."
  "You will not be charged if your video is blocked from generating."

questions.prompt: Which request can you start today without breaking the policy lines in the exhibit?

options.text: A, because a famous face makes the ad stronger.
options.explanation: The policy forbids impersonating an individual without explicit disclosure, in order to deceive. The client asks for both: no deal and no AI label.

options.text: B, because the photos are only references, not part of the final ad.
options.explanation: Gemini's docs ask you to have the necessary rights to any images you upload. A reference is still an upload. License the photos first.

options.text: C: a video made from the studio's own product photos.
options.explanation: Right. The studio shot the photos, so it can upload them. Nothing in the exhibit forbids a product video.

options.text: D, because metadata is only a technical detail.
options.explanation: The goal is to claim a human made the images, in order to deceive. The policy names that: misrepresenting the provenance of generated content.

questions.prompt: Veo blocks a test prompt for request A. A teammate suggests another way. Which plan fits the policies?

options.text: Describe the player without his name, with clues, so the filter misses it.
options.explanation: The policy forbids "circumvention of abuse protections or safety filters". And a look-alike meant to make viewers think it is him, with no AI disclosure, is close to the impersonation line too.

options.text: Retry the same prompt many times. Blocked videos are free.
options.explanation: Blocked videos are not charged, but the prompt still breaks the policy. Trying again does not fix that.

options.text: Send a photo of the player as a reference image instead.
options.explanation: The rights problem stays. You need the necessary rights to any image you upload, and the policy still forbids deceptive impersonation.

options.text: Tell the client you can't make A as asked. Offer a model or athlete who agrees to appear, or an invented character.
options.explanation: Right. Change the brief, not the filter. A person who agrees to appear, or a character who is no real person, avoids the impersonation line in the exhibit.

questions.prompt: Later, the client runs an OpenAI provenance check on a social post made with another vendor's model. The result is not_detected. The client says: "Good, so it's proof our team made it." What do you say?

options.text: Agree. not_detected means a person made it.
options.explanation: OpenAI's docs say a not_detected result does not rule that out: the tool doesn't detect content from another company's AI model.

options.text: It is not proof. OpenAI's check looks only for OpenAI's signals, and metadata can be lost when a file is edited or shared.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says the check isn't a general-purpose AI detector, and that editing, converting or sharing a file can remove its metadata.

options.text: Ask Claude to look at the post and confirm it isn't AI-made.
options.explanation: Claude's docs say it cannot determine whether an image is AI-generated and might be wrong if asked.

options.text: Run the check again until it says detected.
options.explanation: Running it again won't add signals that are not in the file. The check finds only OpenAI's signals.
